name: Emotional Language
definition: Language that contains strong emotional terms – especially those with a negative affect such as fear or outrage.
alsoKnownAs: Fearmongering (a subset of emotional language focused on frightening the listener)
examples: What you're about to see will horrify you
You'll be shocked by what your doctor is keeping from you
The judge issued a DISGUSTING ruling today. It will make your blood boil.
why: Research shows that using emotional words, especially ones that evoke negative emotions such as fear or outrage, increases the viral potential of digital content. Individuals are especially malleable and less focused on rational, deliberate decision making when pushed to a heightened emotional state.
The use of inflammatory language has proven to be especially effective when it comes to spreading ideas over social networks.
whatToDo: Take a moment to arrive at a well-thought-out conclusion or judgment — especially before sharing or responding.
Reflect on your emotional response to content online — if it makes you feel fearful, angry, or distressed, it may be because someone is trying to manipulate you to trigger a reaction.

name: False Dichotomy
definition: Presenting a limited number of choices or sides as mutually exclusive, when in reality more options are possible.
examples: If you're not with us, you're against us
You're either part of the solution or part of the problem
If you vote for X, you won't be able to pay your bills
Either you support the protests or you don't believe in justice.
why: False dichotomy can be a persuasive technique because it artificially narrows choices, making people feel bad if they disagree with the supposedly right choice presented to them. In reality, there may not be clear right and wrong answers.
Furthermore, those who employ false dilemmas will often position the intended/manipulative option as the more desirable of the two (or few) alternatives presented.
whatToDo: Watch out for "either/or," "if this/then that" and other similar statements that imply one of two choices. Most situations are more complex than two outcomes.
Keep an eye out for situations where the existence of other options is denied or concealed.

name: Cherry Picking
definition: Presenting a selection of evidence to support a claim, while ignoring or omitting evidence that contradicts it.
examples: Keeping a live tiger in your apartment is a great way to stop mice
A salesperson who only talks about the features of a product that are most likely to appeal to a specific customer and ignores the features that might not be as appealing
Hot air balloons prove gravity is not real
A scientist who only publishes the results of their research that support their hypothesis and ignores the results that don't
why: Straightforward, simple arguments are compelling, and can be persuasive when compared to a more complex reality that full data would reveal. Even individuals who are well informed can be persuaded by an argument that relies on partial data — but sometimes the most important data is what's not shared.
whatToDo: Try to get a holistic picture of the issue before believing or sharing a single data point.

Be on the lookout for vague statements preceding data. Using words like "many" or "a large amount" could mean that the data isn't being presented accurately. Look to get the details of studies behind the data to make sure you aren't just hearing snippets of information.
Search for the details of studies and data analysis before sharing.
Compare how different sources report the data.

name: Fake Experts
definition: Individuals who speak in a way that conveys the impression of expertise on a topic while possessing little to no relevant expertise. They are often deployed to elicit support for miracle cures, unproven arguments, or to cast doubt on established expert consensus and may leverage entirely fabricated institutions that sound legitimate to add to their guise of credibility.
examples: An influencer wearing a white doctor's coat giving advice about brain cancer
Nutrition advice from a fitness influencer who lost 50 pounds
A philosopher who asserts claims about climate change and emphasizes their doctorate degree, but has not studied climate science
why: Our minds devise shortcuts to help manage vast amounts of information that we process every minute. An ingrained trust in experts is a mental shortcut — instead of having to deal with complicated cognitive decisions to deduce our perspective on a subject we know little about.
But expert credentials can be misleading, especially when an expert's exact background is not clear. Very often audiences fail to verify an expert's background, and take people at their word.
whatToDo: Be on the lookout for experts who appeal to their own authority while contradicting the consensus of others in the field (e.g.: "Trust me, I'm a doctor")
Investigate an expert's background and expertise. Have they studied the specific subject they are commenting on? Have they released peer reviewed research?
Evaluate the institution they work for, including its sources of funding.

name: Appeal to Authority
definition: Citing an authority figure or institution to settle an argument, regardless of whether the authority has relevant expertise on the specific topic at hand. Unlike Fake Experts, the authority may be genuine but is being invoked outside their area of competence or to shut down legitimate debate.
examples: A Nobel Prize-winning physicist says this economic policy is the best, so it must be true
The CEO of a major tech company says vaccines are dangerous — he's a genius, so he must know
My professor said it, so it's definitely correct and there's no point discussing further
This famous athlete endorses this supplement, so it must work
why: People tend to defer to authority figures due to perceived expertise or status, even when the authority's knowledge doesn't extend to the topic in question. This shortcut bypasses critical evaluation of the actual argument.
Appeals to authority can also be used to silence dissent — if a respected figure has spoken, questioning them feels inappropriate, even when the evidence warrants it.
whatToDo: Ask whether the authority being cited has specific, relevant expertise on the topic at hand — not just general prestige or fame.
Remember that even genuine experts can be wrong, especially outside their field. Evaluate the argument on its merits, not just who is making it.
Look for whether a consensus of experts agrees, rather than relying on a single authority's opinion.

name: Red Herring
definition: Diverting attention from a real issue by focusing on a topic with only a surface relevance to the original.
examples: Jack: 'Bob Dylan was the greatest songwriter.' Jill: 'No, Fleetwood Mac had the greatest live performers of all time.'
Why are you upset? Think of all the starving children around the world who have it worse than you.
We shouldn't worry about pollution in our city — there are countries with far worse environmental problems.
Why are we debating school lunches when there are children who don't even have schools?
why: When subtlety isn't an option, a red herring may be employed to confuse the audience. By pivoting to an entirely unrelated, outrageous, and highly charged topic, a speaker can make the audience forget the original discussion.
Some red herrings will subtly switch contexts, retaining superficial similarity between the new and original topic to minimize people's ability to detect a context switch.
whatToDo: Be skeptical when someone responds to a controversial question by calling attention to another charged or polarized topic without actually answering the original question.
Ask yourself: Does this answer the question? Red herrings are meant to distract from the original topic; it could be worth re-asking the question.

name: Scapegoating
definition: Singling out a person or group and placing unwarranted blame on them for a particular problem.
examples: Voter turnout is low because one group refuses to go out and vote.
Unemployment is high because the economy is controlled by one ethnic group.
why: Scapegoating drastically simplifies a complicated issue by diverting attention somewhere else. It allows the perpetrator to redirect attention off themselves and toward another group or person.
whatToDo: Be skeptical of arguments that cast blame on a person or group.
Be wary when you see a serious/complex problem reduced to the fault of an individual or a single group of individuals.

name: Ad Hominem
definition: Attacking a person making an argument, instead of addressing the argument itself. Ad hominem attacks are commonly used to redirect the listener away from the subject at hand and towards an individual.
examples: During a political debate, one candidate claims no one should trust his opponent to lead a foreign policy because he failed a math class once.
A headline calling attention to a candidate's 'screechy' voice during a rally instead of addressing the person's arguments.
why: Ad hominem attacks are arguments that use emotional appeal rather than logic. They're used with the explicit intent of redirecting the listener away from the topic at hand, which might be hard to poke holes in, and towards the "flaws" of an individual or entity, which might be easier.
Ad hominem attacks work because once an individual agrees that the holder of the point of view is flawed, it can become harder for them to agree that their point of view is not.
whatToDo: Be skeptical of arguments that question (or attack) the shortcomings of a person or entity, rather than the merits of their argument.
Watch out for attempts at downplaying an argument due to the person's/entity's negative characteristics or limitations.

name: Polarization
definition: Dividing into two sharply contrasting groups or opinions. A state in which the opinions, beliefs, or interests of a group or society no longer range along a continuum but become concentrated at opposing extremes.
examples: Don't believe the other party's lies. They said they care about workers but more people are out of work than ever.
I don't trust people from the other team. They're lazy and cheat.
why: It preys on the tendency of people with strong beliefs to dislike and distrust those different from themselves.
Hostile 'othering' language can reinforce biases, separating and dividing groups even further.
whatToDo: Be skeptical of arguments that cast blame on a person or group.
Be wary when you see a serious/complex problem reduced to blame on an individual or a single group of individuals.

name: Slippery Slope
definition: Asserting that a first step taken will inevitably lead to major, often disastrous, consequences.
examples: If we implement even a modest change in policy, we'll lose all of our freedoms.
If you don't pass tomorrow's math test, then you can't take calculus next year. If you don't take calculus, you won't get into college!
If we allow students to redo one test, soon they'll expect to redo every assignment, and eventually no one will study at all.
why: Slippery slope arguments take advantage of the gray area between initial actions and their conclusions. They often rely on fear of grave – and unavoidable – consequences of any step taken and can bypass more critical evaluations of the arguments they present.
whatToDo: Consider the emotional aspect of the argument. If the predicted consequences are portrayed as dire or frightening, it's possible someone may be trying to manipulate you.
Evaluate the likelihood that consequences would inevitably follow from a first step. Consider the other events that would have to take place and whether or not other outcomes might be possible.

name: Decontextualization
definition: Intentionally showing text, audio, or visuals in a different context or removing important background information in order to change its meaning.
examples: A photo of damage from a natural disaster posted with a misleading comment asserting the damage was caused by a recent protest
Selectively edited audio or video of an individual that makes their comments appear to have a different meaning
why: Removing context from a piece of content can lead to people being misinformed and forming their opinions based on misleading information.
It preys on the tendency of people to trust their eyes and ears, which often overrides the impulse to confirm or fact check with other sources.
whatToDo: Be skeptical of arguments that rely on a highly inflammatory image or quote and always double check the source sharing the information: is it reputable and/or trustworthy?

Review content shared online carefully to determine if the commentary surrounding it is accurate by seeing if others are sharing or refuting the information and/or searching for the original source of the image/video/story. Reverse Image Search is a great tool to find the origin point for images.

name: Hasty Generalization
definition: Drawing a broad conclusion from a small or unrepresentative sample of evidence. One or a few examples are treated as proof of a universal rule.
examples: I met two rude people from that city, so everyone there must be rude.
My friend got food poisoning at that restaurant, so the whole chain must be unsafe.
One study found a link between X and Y, so X definitely causes Y.
This politician lied once, so you can never trust anything any politician says.
why: Our brains are wired to find patterns quickly, which helped in survival situations but can mislead in complex modern contexts. A single vivid example can feel more convincing than a mountain of statistics, leading people to generalize from limited experience.
Hasty generalizations are especially effective because they offer simple, memorable narratives that are easy to share and hard to argue against without detailed counter-evidence.
whatToDo: Ask how large and representative the sample is. One or two examples rarely prove a universal rule.
Look for counter-examples. If the conclusion is 'all X are Y,' can you find even one X that isn't Y?
Be wary of language like 'always,' 'never,' 'everyone,' or 'no one' — these signal potential overgeneralization.

name: Appeal to Majority
definition: Arguing that something must be true or good because many people believe it or do it. The popularity of an idea is treated as evidence of its correctness.
examples: Millions of people use this product, so it must be the best one available.
Most people believe this policy is right, so it must be the correct approach.
Everyone is investing in this stock — you'd be foolish not to join them.
This is the most popular opinion online, so it's clearly the truth.
why: Humans are social creatures with a deep instinct to conform to group behavior. When we see large numbers of people supporting something, we tend to assume the group has done the evaluation for us and follow along.
This tactic is especially potent in digital environments where metrics like likes, shares, and follower counts create visible 'social proof' that can be easily manufactured or manipulated.
whatToDo: Remember that popularity doesn't equal truth. Many widely held beliefs throughout history have turned out to be wrong.
Evaluate the claim on its own evidence and logic, independent of how many people support it.
Consider whether the 'majority' claim is even accurate — stated numbers can be exaggerated or fabricated.

name: Appeal to Nature
definition: Arguing that something is good, right, or superior simply because it is 'natural,' or that something is bad because it is 'unnatural' or synthetic.
examples: This remedy is made from all-natural ingredients, so it must be safer than medicine.
Humans weren't meant to eat processed food — if it's not natural, it's not good for you.
Traditional farming is better because it's how nature intended food to be grown.
You shouldn't take that medication — it's full of chemicals. Try this herbal alternative instead.
why: People tend to associate 'natural' with 'safe' and 'good,' even though many natural substances are harmful (e.g., arsenic, snake venom) and many synthetic ones are beneficial (e.g., vaccines, clean water treatment).
This fallacy exploits a romanticized view of nature and a distrust of modern technology, making it particularly effective in health, food, and environmental discussions.
whatToDo: Ask whether something being 'natural' actually makes it safe or effective. Naturalness alone is not evidence of quality.
Look for actual evidence of safety, efficacy, or superiority — not just claims about origin.
Remember that 'natural' and 'chemical' are not opposites. Everything is made of chemicals, and many natural substances are dangerous.

name: Appeal to Tradition
definition: Arguing that something is right, good, or should continue simply because it has been done that way for a long time. The age of a practice is treated as evidence of its value.
examples: We've always done it this way, and it's worked fine. There's no reason to change now.
This teaching method has been used for centuries — it's stood the test of time.
Our ancestors knew best. Modern approaches are just fads that will pass.
Marriage has always been defined this way, so we shouldn't redefine it.
why: Tradition provides comfort and a sense of stability. People often assume that practices which have persisted for a long time must have survived because they work, even though many outdated practices persist due to habit, cultural inertia, or lack of alternatives.
Appealing to tradition also evokes emotional attachments to identity and heritage, making it harder to question the practice without feeling like you're attacking the community itself.
whatToDo: Ask whether the tradition is actually effective, or whether it simply persists because 'that's how it's always been done.'
Consider whether the circumstances that justified the tradition still apply today.
Recognize that many positive social changes required breaking with tradition — longevity alone doesn't make something right.
